clips.L1-P1-S1: Hi, is this Greg? It's Nadia Rahimi in Unit 1204. I'm sorry to call so early, but there's water coming through my bathroom ceiling. Good morning, Nadia. No problem, that's what I'm here for. How much water are we talking about? It's a steady drip, maybe one drop every second, right above the bathtub. There's a brown stain about the size of a dinner plate, and it seems to be getting bigger. Okay. Above the tub is actually the best place for it, because the water's going straight down the drain. Is the ceiling sagging at all, like it's bulging down? No, it's flat. Just wet. Good. Then it's probably not dangerous. The unit above you is 1304. The owners are away in Portugal until the end of the month, but I have a key. Most likely it's their bathtub or the toilet supply line. I'll go up there right now and check. Thank you. I have to leave for work at 8.30, though. That's fine. You don't need to be home for me to get into 1304.
clips.L1-P1-S2: Nadia, it's Greg again. I found it. The pipe that feeds the toilet in 1304 had a crack in it, so water was spraying behind the toilet and soaking into the floor. I've turned off the water to that toilet, so the leak should stop within the hour once the floor dries out a bit. That's a relief. What about my ceiling, though? The stain's pretty ugly. The drywall will need to dry completely first. If we paint it too early, the stain just comes back through the paint. I'll bring you a fan this evening to speed things up. Give it about a week. And who pays for the repair? I don't want this coming out of my pocket. In a case like this, it usually goes through the building's insurance, because the pipe failed on its own. Nobody did anything wrong. But there's a deductible, and the condo board decides how that's shared. I'll put it on the agenda for the next meeting.
clips.L1-P1-S3: Greg, one more thing. My bathroom fan has been making a rattling noise for weeks. While someone's here, could they look at that too? Sure, but just so you know, the fan is inside your unit, so it's your responsibility, not the buildings. I can give you the name of the electrician we use. He charges about $90 to come out. $90 just to show up. That includes the first half hour. Honestly, it's often just dust in the motor. Try cleaning the cover with a vacuum first. If it's still rattling after that, give him a call. Okay, I'll try that tonight. Thanks for being so quick this morning. No problem. I'll drop the fan off around six.
clips.L1-P2: Layla, did you see the poster for the harvest run? It's on the 12th of October, along the river path. I did. Are you thinking of doing it? I was thinking we could do it together. There's a 5 kilometer run and a 10 kilometer run. Five, definitely. I haven't run more than three kilometers since the spring. That's fair. Registration is $35 before the end of September, and $45 after that. The money goes to the children's hospital. Then let's sign up this weekend so we get the lower price. But if we're doing this, I need a plan. I can't just show up and hope. How about we train on Tuesday and Thursday mornings before work and do a longer run on Sundays? We've got six weeks. Mornings are hard for me. Could we do evenings instead? I'm much more awake after work. Sure, evenings it is. We can meet at the footbridge at 6.30. Perfect. And I need new shoes. Mine are falling apart. Go to the running store on Elm Street. They watch you run on a treadmill and suggest the right kind.
clips.L1-P3: Hi, I'm planning to take my two kids fishing at Pine Lake next month, and I'm not sure what licenses we need. Happy to help. How old are the children? 8 and 13. Then they don't need anything. In this province, anyone under 16 can fish without a license, as long as they're with an adult who has one. So it's just you. Great! Where do I get it? Almost everyone buys it online now. It takes about 10 minutes. You'll need a valid ID, and you'll have to print the license or keep it on your phone. Officers can ask to see it at any time. What does it cost? An annual license for a resident is $28. If you only fish once or twice a year, there's also a one-day license for 12, but if you're going more than twice, the annual one is better value. We'll probably go three or four times this summer. Then the annual license makes sense. One more thing, Pine Lake has special rules. You can keep up to for walleye a day, but any walleye longer than 50 centimeters has to go back in the water. Those are the big breeding fish. How would I know how long it is? Most people bring a measuring tape. There's also a measuring board on the dock at the boat launch. Good to know. Can we use live minnows as bait? Not at Pine Lake. Live bait fish are banned there to keep other species out of the lake. Worms are fine, though, and so are lures.
clips.L1-P4: Residents of Lakeview who need a power drill, a sewing machine, or even a telescope no longer have to buy one. Starting next Monday, the Lakeview Public Library will open what it calls a Library of Things at its main street branch. The new collection includes more than 200 items from camping stoves and snowshoes to board games and a professional quality camera. Anyone with a free library card can borrow up to two items at a time for one week. Head librarian Marisa Cuallo says the idea came from the library's own survey last year, in which many residents said they wanted to try a hobby but could not afford the equipment. Most people use a drill for maybe 15 minutes in its whole life, she said. It makes more sense for a community to share one. The project cost about $40,000, most of it paid by a provincial grant for programs that reduce waste. Local businesses donated some of the larger items, including a pressure washer and two kayaks. Late fees will not apply, but borrowers who damage an item will be asked to pay for repairs. The library says it plans to add more items in the spring, based on requests from users.
clips.L1-P5: Thanks for staying after the meeting. We need to choose this year's fundraiser for the new playground. The two ideas on the table are a fun run and a spring market. Paul, you suggested the fun run. Right. Kids collect pledges from family and neighbors for every lap they run around the field. It's healthy, it's simple to organize, and last year Oak Ridge School raised nearly $11,000 that way. I like that it gets the kids moving, but I'm a bit uncomfortable with pledges. Some families can ask a lot of relatives for money, and others can't ask anyone. The kids notice who raises the most, and the ones who raise nothing feel bad. That's a fair point. We could stop announcing individual totals and only share the class totals. That helps. But I'd still rather do the market. Families rent a table for $20 and sell crafts, baking or use toys, and we sell food. Everyone can take part, even if they have no money to give. How much did the market raise when we did it three years ago? About 4,000. But that year it rained and we had it in the gym. Outdoors, with more tables, I think we could double it. Even doubled, that's less than the fun run. And a market needs far more volunteers on the day, tables, cash boxes, the food stand, cleanup. Volunteers are my biggest worry. Last year, we struggled to find 10 people for the bake sale. Then what about doing both, but small? The fun run in the morning, and a few food and craft tables in the afternoon, at the same event. Families who come to watch the run will already be there to shop. I could live with that, as long as the run is the main event. I like it. It's one day of volunteers instead of two. Paul, could you draft a pledge form without individual rankings? Hiroko, could you find out how many families would want a table? I'll send a survey home on Friday.
clips.L1-P6: Drive through almost any Canadian city in summer and you'll see the same thing, neat, short grass in every park, along every boulevard and around every highway ramp. Keeping it that way costs a fortune. Some cities spend millions of dollars a year on mowing, and the mowers themselves burn a surprising amount of fuel. That's why a growing number of municipalities are trying something called naturalization. Instead of mowing everything, they let selected areas grow long, sometimes planting native wildflowers and grasses. Supporters point out three benefits. First, it saves money and fuel. Second, longer grass and wildflowers give bees and butterflies the food and shelter they've been losing. And third, deep-rooted native plants soak up rainwater, which helps reduce flooding after storms. Not everyone is convinced. Some residents complain that unmowed areas look messy, like the city has simply given up. Others worry about ticks, which can carry Lyme disease and tend to live in long grass. Those are real concerns, and I don't think cities should dismiss them. But I think the answer lies in where and how it's done. Nobody is suggesting we stop mowing soccer fields or the lawn beside the playground. The best programs keep a mown strip along every path, so people can walk without brushing against long grass, and they put up signs explaining what's being grown and why. When people understand that the long grass is a choice, not neglect, most of the complaints disappear. So my view is this, cities should naturalize the places where people rarely walk, such as highway ramps, steep slopes and the far edges of large parks, and keep mowing the places where people actually play.
clips.L2-P1-S1: Hi, I was booked on the 640 flight to Winnipeg tonight, and the board just says, cancelled. Can you tell me what's going on? I'm very sorry, sir. There's a mechanical problem with the aircraft, and a replacement part won't arrive until tomorrow. Can I have your booking code? It's KL7Q2M. Thank you. I can put you on the first flight tomorrow morning, which leaves at 7.15 and lands at 9.05. Or there's a flight tonight through Calgary, but you'd land in Winnipeg at 1.30 in the morning. Through Calgary tonight? That's a long night. What about the morning flight? Is it full? It's getting full, but I have a few seats left. Since the cancellation is our fault, the airline will pay for a hotel tonight and give you a meal voucher. Okay, the morning flight, then. I'd rather sleep in a real bed than in an airport.
clips.L2-P1-S2: All right, you're confirmed on the 7.15. Here is your hotel voucher. The hotel is the skyline in, and there's a free shuttle from door number 8 every 20 minutes. Great. What about my suitcase? I checked it a couple of hours ago. Your bag will stay in the system and go on tomorrow's flight automatically. You don't need to collect it. The thing is, my medication is in that suitcase. I need to take it tonight and tomorrow morning. Ah, then we'll need to get it back for you. That can take about 45 minutes. Go to the baggage service office on the lower level, show them this tag number, and they'll bring it out. Just remember to check it in again tomorrow at the counter, not at the gate. 45 minutes is fine. Better than missing my medication.
clips.L2-P1-S3: One more question. I was supposed to be at my sister's engagement party in Winnipeg tonight. I'm going to miss it completely. Is there any compensation for that? Because this was a mechanical problem within our control, you may be eligible for compensation under the federal passenger rules. For a delay like yours, it's usually a few hundred dollars. How do I claim it? You need to submit a claim on our website within one year. Keep your boarding pass and this cancellation notice. We have 30 days to answer you. All right. I'll do that once I'm home. Thanks for your help.
clips.L2-P2: Mike your mom called. She's not feeling great and she asked if we could visit this weekend instead of next month Is it serious? She said it's just a bad cold, but she sounded tired and a bit lonely. I think she'd really like to see the kids Then let's go the drive to Brandon is only two and a half hours Saturday morning Saturday works, but Emma has her swimming lesson at 9 We can leave right after at 10 30. We'd be there for lunch Good I'll make a big pot of soup tonight that we can take with us. So she doesn't have to cook She'll like that. Should we stay over? Let's see how she's doing if she's tired. We'll drive back the same evening If she's feeling better, we'll stay until Sunday and help with her garden She said the leaves need raking Sounds like a plan. I'll call her now to let her know we're coming
clips.L2-P3: Hello, I heard the city opened a new recycling depot. I have a lot of stuff from cleaning out my basement, and I'm not sure what goes where. You've come to the right place. The new Eco Center on Industrial Road takes many things your curbside bins can't. Old electronics, paint, batteries, scrap metal, and large pieces of cardboard. I have an old TV and two computer monitors. Electronics are free to drop off. There's no limit. And some half empty cans of paint. Paint is also free, as long as it's in the original can with the label. If you poured it into another container, they can't accept it, because they don't know what's inside. What about an old mattress? Mattresses are accepted, but there's a fee of $20 each, because they're expensive to take apart. Okay. When is it open? Tuesday to Saturday, 8 to 5. It's closed Sundays and Mondays. Saturdays get very busy, so if you can, go on a weekday. Do I need to bring anything? Just a utility bill or your driver's license to show you live in the city. The depot is only for residents. Businesses have to use the commercial site.
clips.L2-P4: Students in the small northern town of Elk Ridge will soon have Fridays off. The local school board voted last night to move its two schools to a four-day week starting in September, making it one of the first districts in the province to try the idea. Under the plan, the school day will be about 45 minutes longer from Monday to Thursday, so students will spend the same total number of hours in class. The board says the main reason is a shortage of teachers. The two schools have had trouble filling positions for three years in a row, and board chair Denise Arkane says a four-day week will help attract new teachers to the remote community. Some parents have raised concerns about child care. Not every family can stay home on a Friday, said one mother at the meeting. In response, the board has partnered with the community center to offer a low-cost Friday day camp with sports, crafts and homework help. The board will review the change after one year, looking at attendance, test results and how many teaching positions have been filled.
clips.L2-P5: So, everyone agrees we're doing the reunion in July. The question is where? Last time, we were in my backyard, and honestly, 40 people was too many for it. I've been looking at the Group Picnic site at Birds Hill Park. It has a big shelter with tables, barbecues, washrooms and a playground. It's $90 for the day. That sounds lovely, but it's 45 minutes out of the city. Grandpa doesn't like long car rides anymore, and half the cousins don't have cars. We could organize rides. I have a van that seats 7. Maybe. My idea was the community hall on Dufferin Avenue. It's 10 minutes from most of us, it has a kitchen, and it's air conditioned. Remember how hot it was last July. I remember grandpa had to sit inside the whole afternoon. But the hall costs $300, and the kids can't run around inside. Half the fun of a reunion is the kids playing outside together. There's a small park right across the street from the hall. The kids could go back and forth with a couple of adults. That's not bad. What do the rules say about food? Last time, everyone brought a dish. The hall allows potlucks. You just need to clean the kitchen afterward. The park allows potlucks too, obviously. And cooking burgers outside is part of the tradition. I think grandpa's comfort matters most. He's 91, and this might be one of the last reunions he can really enjoy. You're right. I hadn't thought about it that way. The hall it is. But I'm bringing a portable barbecue for the parking lot. As long as it's allowed, fine. I'll call the hall tomorrow and ask about that, and about booking the third Saturday in July.
clips.L2-P6: One of the first questions many newcomers to Canada ask me is, should I buy a car? It's an understandable question. In much of the country, distances are large, winters are hard, and public transit outside the big cities can be limited. A car can feel like the key to freedom. But my advice, in most cases, is to wait at least a few months. Here's why. First, the cost is much higher than people expect. It isn't just the price of the car. Insurance for a new driver with no Canadian driving history can cost several hundred dollars a month, sometimes more than the car payment itself. Add gas, winter tires, parking and repairs, and many families are surprised by the total. Second, many newcomers can't use their foreign license for long. In most provinces, you can drive on it for a limited time, usually a few months, and then you must pass Canadian tests. If you buy a car first, you may end up paying for it while you wait for a road test. Third, you don't yet know where you'll live or work. Many people move apartments or change jobs in their first year. A car that seemed essential for one commute may be unnecessary after the next move. That said, I'm not against cars. In small towns or for shift workers whose jobs start before the buses run, a car may be necessary from day one. My point is simply that it shouldn't be an automatic decision. Try transit, car sharing and carpooling first. Get your license sorted out. Then, if you still need a car, you'll be in a much better position to choose one.
clips.L3-P1-S1: Hi, this is Lucia Ferrero. I'm supposed to start as an accounts assistant today, but I'm at the front desk of your front street office, and the receptionist says no one is expecting me. Hi, Lucia. This is Mark from HR. I'm so sorry about that. Can you hold on one second? Ah, I see the problem. Your team moved to our King Street office last week, and your welcome letter still had the old address. Oh, no. How far is King Street? About 15 minutes on foot, or two stops on the streetcar. Your manager, Helen, is there now. I'll call her and let her know you're on your way. Okay. Should I still bring my documents? I have my banking information and my social insurance number with me. Yes, please. We'll need both to set up your pay. But don't rush. Your first meeting isn't until 10.
clips.L3-P1-S2: Hi Mark, it's Lucie again. I'm at King Street now, and Helen's been great. But there's another small problem. My computer login doesn't work. Hmm. Did you use the temporary password from your letter? Yes, but it says my account is locked. That happens if someone types the wrong password three times. It might have been the IT team testing it. Accounts unlock automatically after 30 minutes, but I can ask IT to unlock it now. That would be great, because Helen wants me to join a training session at 11. Done. I've sent the request. While you wait, can you fill in the paper forms Helen gave you? There for your benefits, like your dental plan. You need to return them within 30 days, but it's easier to do it while you're there.
clips.L3-P1-S3: Last thing, I promise. Helen mentioned a parking pass, but I usually take transit. Is there any help with transit costs? Yes, actually. The company pays half of a monthly transit pass. You buy the pass, keep the receipt, and submit it with your expense claim at the end of each month. That's great. Is there a form for that? It's all online. Once your login works, look for expenses on the staff home page. The first claim can include this month, even though you started partway through. Perfect. Thanks for sorting everything out, Mark.
clips.L3-P2: Jamal, you look stressed. What's up? My phone contract ends next week, and I have to choose a new plan. There are about 20 options, and they all look the same. What do you actually use your phone for? Mostly messages and maps. I watch videos at home on Wi-Fi, so I don't need much data on the go. Then don't pay for the big plans. I'm on a prepaid plan with 10 GB for $35 a month, and I never run out. Prepaid. Isn't that for people with bad credit? Not at all. A lot of people use it now. You pay at the start of each month, there's no contract, and you can switch anytime if you find something cheaper. That sounds better than being locked in for two years. But what about calls to my parents in Morocco? I call them every Sunday. Don't use your phone plan for that. International calls are expensive. Use a free calling app over Wi-Fi instead. I talk to my sister in Chile every week that way. Good idea. I'll look at prepaid plans tonight.
clips.L3-P3: Hi, I'm interested in renting a plot in the community garden on Spruce Street. How does it work? Great. We have two sizes. A small plot is about 3 meters by 3 meters and costs $40 for the season. A large plot is twice that size and costs $70. I've never gardened before. Which would you recommend? For a beginner, I always suggest the small one. It's easy to keep under control. People who start with a large plot often find the weeds when by August. That makes sense. Is water included? Yes. There are taps and hoses at both ends of the garden. We just ask people not to water in the middle of the day when most of it evaporates. Early morning or evening is best. And tools? There's a shared shed with shovels, rakes and wheelbarrows. The code for the lock is given out at the orientation session. Is the orientation required? It is. It's on the first Saturday in May at 10. We go over the rules, show people where things are, and give out the plot numbers. What are the main rules? Only organic gardening, so no chemical sprays. Every gardener also does for hours of volunteer work during the season, helping with shared areas like the paths and the compost. And if a plot is left completely untended for three weeks, we may give it to someone on the waiting list.
clips.L3-P4: A family bakery in Halifax has found a new way to deal with leftover bread. Instead of throwing it out at closing time, Harbicide Bakery now puts all-unsulled loaves on a free shelf outside its front door every evening at seven. Owner Thomas LeBlanc says the bakery used to throw away about 30 loaves a day. It broke my heart, he said. Good bread, baked that morning, going into the garbage. Anyone can take bread from the shelf, no questions asked, but the bakery asks people to take only what they need. A sign on the shelf reminds visitors that it is there for everyone. Since the program started in March, LeBlanc says almost no bread has been wasted. He also says his sales have gone up, not down, because people who first came for free bread have become paying customers. The idea has spread. Two other bakeries in the city have started similar shelves, and a local grocery store is now considering doing the same with fruit and vegetables.
clips.L3-P5: Ok, last item. Several people have asked if we could allow dogs in the office one day a week. Ben, you brought it up first. Yes. My dog, Max, is alone for nine hours on the days I'm in the office, and I hate it. I've read that offices with dog days have happier staff and lower stress. A few companies downtown already do it. I'm happy for people who have dogs, but I have to be honest, I'm allergic. Not badly, but if there are three or four dogs on our floor, I'll be sneezing all day. I didn't know that. I'm sorry. It's okay. And it's not just me. Some people are afraid of dogs, especially if they've been bitten before. They might not say anything, but they'd be uncomfortable. Those are important points. Is there a way to do this that works for everyone? What if dogs were only allowed in one area, like the meeting room at the end of the hall, and not near anyone's desk? That might help, but the allergens travel. They get on clothes and furniture. What about the building rules? Has anyone checked? I did. The building allows it as long as the dogs are vaccinated on a leash in the hallways, and the owner takes responsibility for any damage. Here's another idea. Instead of bringing dogs here, what if Ben and others could work from home one extra day a week? Then Max isn't alone and nobody's allergic. Honestly, that would solve my problem better. Max would be happier at home than in a strange office. I like that, but I can't decide it alone. Working from home is a company policy. I'll take the idea to the director on Monday and ask for a three-month trial for people with pets.
clips.L3-P6: A few years ago, I tipped when someone served me a meal at a table, and that was about it. Today, I'm asked to tip almost everywhere, at the coffee counter, at the self-checkout of a frozen yogurt shop, even when I pick up a takeout order myself. The payment screen turns toward me with options of 18, 20 or 25%, and I feel the cashier watching. Many Canadians feel the same way. Surveys show that most people think tipping has gotten out of hand. And yet most of us keep tipping partly out of habit and partly because we know that service workers don't earn much. That second reason is the heart of the problem. In many workplaces, tips aren't really a reward for excellent service. They're part of how the business pays its staff. The customer, in effect, is asked to cover part of the wage that the employer chooses not to pay. Some restaurants in Canada have tried a different model. They raise their menu prices by about 15%, pay staff a better hourly wage, and tell customers that no tip is expected. The results have been mixed. Staff often earn more reliable income, but some customers see the higher prices and go elsewhere, not realizing that the final bill is about the same. I don't think we should abolish tipping overnight. Many workers depend on it, and they could lose income if it disappeared without a plan. But I'd like to see two changes. First, tip screens should start with a no tip option that isn't hidden. Second, more businesses should include fair wages and their prices and say so clearly. Then a tip could go back to being what it was meant to be, a thank you for great service, not a hidden part of the bill.
clips.L4-P1-S1: Hi Diane, it's Kenji. I'm calling about the apartment on Gladstone Avenue. I saw it last night, and I'd really like to rent it. Oh, that's wonderful news, Kenji. I had two other people interested, but I like that you asked so many careful questions. Thanks. There's just one thing. When I looked in the bedroom closet, I noticed some black spots on the back wall, near the floor. I think it might be mold. Hemmum. That closet is on an outside wall. In winter, it gets cold in there, and sometimes there's a bit of moisture. I can have it cleaned before you move in. I'd appreciate that, but I'm worried it'll just come back. My daughter has asthma, so mold is a real concern for us. I understand completely. Let me ask my contractor to come and look at it properly this week, so we know what's causing it. I don't want to just paint over a problem.
clips.L4-P1-S2: Kenji, it's Dianne. My contractor, Roll, looked at the closet this morning. Good news and bad news. Okay, bad news first. The insulation behind that wall is too thin, so warm air from inside meets the cold wall and turns to water. That's what's feeding the mold. To fix it properly, Roll needs to open the wall, add insulation and close it up again. How long would that take? About four days, and he can't start until the 15th. Your move-in date was the first. And the good news? The mold is only on the surface of the dry wall. It hasn't spread inside the wall, so it's not dangerous, and once the insulation is fixed, it shouldn't come back.
clips.L4-P1-S3: So what do you suggest about the move-in date? I have two options for you. You could move in on the first as planned and keep the bedroom closet empty and closed until the work is done. Or you could move in on the 19th, after the repair, and I wouldn't charge you rent for those first 18 days. Our currently sends on the 31st, so we have nowhere to live for almost three weeks. Then the first option is probably better. I'll take $100 off the first month's rent for the trouble, and Rowe will keep the noise to working hours. That's fair. Let's do that.
clips.L4-P2: Raj, did you see the big branch from the Henderson's Maple? It's hanging right over our garage roof. I saw it this morning. After last night's wind, it's cracked halfway through. If it falls, it'll go straight through the shingles. Should we cut it ourselves? You have that saw in the shed. No way. It's too high, and it's their tree. If something goes wrong, we'd be responsible. Besides, I'm not climbing a ladder in this wind. Fair enough. Then let's talk to the Henderson's. Mrs. Henderson is always home in the afternoon. Good idea. I'll go over at lunch. They're nice people. I'm sure they'll want to deal with it. And if they can't afford a tree service, that can cost a few hundred dollars. Then we could offer to share the cost. It's cheaper than fixing a roof. Agreed. And take a photo of the branch first, just in case we ever need it for insurance. I'll do that now, before I forget.
clips.L4-P3: Good morning. My family just arrived in Canada last week. Someone told me the library could help us. Welcome. Yes, we can help in lots of ways. First, everyone in your family can get a free library card. You just need one piece of ID and something with your address on it, like a lease or a letter from a bank. We have our passports and our lease. That's perfect. Children under 12 get a card too, but a parent has to sign for them. My son is 14. Does he need me? No, at 14 he can sign for himself. With the card, you can borrow books, movies, and even laptops. We lend laptops for two weeks at a time. That would help a lot. We don't have a computer yet. We also have free English conversation circles every Tuesday and Thursday evening. No registration, just drop in. They're a good way to practice and meet other newcomers. And for my younger daughter? She's 6. We have a homework club after school for ages 6 to 12, Monday to Thursday. That one does need registration because space is limited. I can sign her up today.
clips.L4-P4: Starting next month, riders in the Westwood neighborhood will be able to take a ride on a bus with no driver at the wheel. The city has announced a six-month trial of two small electric self-driving shuttles. Each shuttle carries up to eight passengers and will travel a three-kilometer loop between the Westwood seniors' residence, the community health center and the local shopping plaza. Rides will be free during the trial. Although the shuttles drive themselves, a trained staff member will be on board at all times, ready to take control if needed. The shuttles will travel at a maximum speed of 25 kilometers an hour and will not operate during snowstorms. City transit director Alain Bouchard says the trial is designed to answer one main question. Can small automated vehicles help older residents get around in areas where full-size buses run only once an hour? Not everyone is enthusiastic. The Transit Workers Union has raised concerns about future jobs and some residents worry about safety. The city says it will hold two public meetings during the trial to collect feedback.
clips.L4-P5: As you know, the company has given each team $500 for a team building day before the end of the year. I'd like us to decide today. Any ideas? I'd love to do an escape room. You're locked in a room with puzzles and you have an hour to get out. It really forces people to work together and it's fun. There's a good one downtown and it's about $30 a person. Escape rooms are fun, but I've heard they can be stressful for some people. Small rooms, a countdown clock, people shouting ideas. Not everyone enjoys that. That's true. My cousin had a panic attack in one. My idea is a cooking class. There's a place on Bank Street where groups make a three-course meal together and then eat it. You still have to cooperate, but it's relaxed and everyone gets a good meal at the end. How much is it? $65 a person. With 12 of us, that's $780. That's over the budget. I know. But maybe the company would cover the difference if we skipped the year-end lunch. We usually spend about $300 on that anyway. That's a creative idea. I'd need to check with finance. We should also think about our June. He uses a wheelchair, so whatever we choose has to be fully accessible. I already asked. The cooking school has a ramp and adjustable counters. The escape room is in a basement with stairs, so I guess that settles it. It does, unless finance says no. May, could you send me the cooking school's details? I'll talk to finance this afternoon, and if they approve, we'll book a Friday in early December.
clips.L4-P6: In Ontario, high school students must complete 40 hours of community service before they can graduate. Some other provinces have no such rule, and every few years someone asks whether all of Canada should require it. As a former teacher, I've watched this program up close, and I have mixed feelings. On the positive side, I've seen students discover things about themselves they never would have found in a classroom. A shy girl who volunteered at a senior's home became so confident that she later studied nursing. A boy who helped coach a children's soccer team realized he wanted to be a teacher. For some students, those 40 hours open a door. But for many others, I'm afraid the hours are just a box to tick. In the spring of grade 12, students scramble to find any activity that counts, and some organizations sign the forms without checking how much work was really done. When volunteering is forced and rushed, students don't learn generosity. They learn to see helping others as a chore. There's also a fairness issue. Students who work part-time jobs to support their families, or who look after younger siblings, have much less free time. Yet their responsibilities don't count as community service. So here is what I'd suggest. Keep the requirement but make it more meaningful. Spread the hours over all for years instead of letting them pile up at the end. Let schools count family caregiving and some paid work in special cases. And ask students to write a short reflection about what they learned. 40 hours can be valuable, but only if students have the time, and the reason to take them seriously.
clips.L5-P1-S1: Hi, I bought a used Honda from your lot two weeks ago, and the check engine light came on this morning on my way to work. I'm sorry to hear that. Is the car driving differently at all? Any strange noises, shaking, or loss of power? Not really. Maybe it's a little rough when it's idling at a red light, but I'm not sure. I might just be nervous. That's okay. A steady light usually means it's safe to drive for now. If the light starts flashing, though, pull over and stop the engine, because that can mean serious damage. It's steady, not flashing. Good. Your car came with our 30-day warranty, so you're still covered. Can you bring it in tomorrow morning? We'll plug in our computer and read the error code. Tomorrow at 8 works. How long will it take? Reading the code only takes 20 minutes. If it's something bigger, we'll need the car for the day.
clips.L5-P1-S2: Fatima, it's Eric. We read the code on your car. One of the ignition coils is failing. That's why the engine felt a little rough. It's a common problem on this model. Is it expensive? The part itself is about $150, plus an hour of labor. But since you're under warranty, it's covered. You won't pay anything. That's a relief. When will it be ready? Here's the issue. We don't have the part in stock. It should arrive Thursday, and we can install it Thursday afternoon. Today's Tuesday. I really need a car to get to work. I'm a home care nurse, and I visit four or five clients a day. I understand. Let me see what I can do about a loaner car.
clips.L5-P1-S3: Okay, I have good news. We have one loaner car available, a small Toyota. You can keep it until Thursday afternoon. Thank you so much. Is there any charge? No charge for the car, but you'll need to return it with the same amount of gas, and you'll need to show us proof of insurance before you take it. I have my insurance card in my wallet. Can I pick it up now? Yes. Come to the service desk. And Fatima, since this happened so soon after you bought the car, I'll also give you a free oil change on Thursday. That's very kind. I'll be there in half an hour.
clips.L5-P2: Victor, Sophie's birthday is in three weeks. We need to decide about the party. Last year we had it at home, and 15 kids in our living room was chaos. I know. I was finding cake under the couch for a week. This year, what about the trampoline park? They do party packages. How much? $300 for up to 12 kids, including pizza, and an hour of jumping. That's a lot. What about the community center? They rent the small gym for $80 for two hours. That's cheaper, but we'd have to plan all the games, bring the food and clean up. With the trampoline park, they do everything. True. And Sophie has been talking about trampolines for months. Okay, let's do it. But 12 kids maximum. She'll have to choose. That's fine. She said she only wants her friends from class, and her cousins anyway. I'll call them tomorrow to book a Saturday. You can help her make the invitations.
clips.L5-P3: Hi. I'm thinking of moving my accounts from my big bank to your credit union. Can you explain how it's different? Of course. The biggest difference is ownership. A bank is owned by its shareholders. A credit union is owned by its members, the people who bank here. When you open an account, you buy one membership share for $5, and that makes you a part owner. Does that mean I get a vote? Yes. Every member gets one vote at our annual meeting, no matter how much money they have with us. Interesting. What about fees? My bank charges me $15 a month. Our basic checking account has no monthly fee if you keep at least $1,000 in it. Below that, it's for dollars a month. Can I use my card at any bank machine? You can use any machine in our national network for free. There are about 3,000 of them across Canada. Machines outside the network charge a fee, usually $2 or $3. Is my money as safe here as at a bank? Yes. Deposits are protected by the provincial deposit guarantee, just like bank deposits are protected federally. Okay. What do I need to open an account? Two pieces of ID, one with a photo, and your social insurance number. It takes about 30 minutes, and you can do it here or online.
clips.L5-P4: Environment Canada has issued a heat warning for the city, beginning tomorrow and expected to last at least three days. Daytime temperatures are forecast to reach 34 degrees, and with humidity, it will feel closer to 40. Nights will stay unusually warm, around 22 degrees, which gives the body little chance to recover. Health officials say older adults, young children and people with chronic illnesses are most at risk. They are urging residents to drink water often, even before they feel thirsty, and to check on elderly neighbors and relatives who live alone. To help, the city will open six cooling centers in community centers and libraries. They will stay open until 11 at night, two hours later than usual. Outdoor pools will also have extended hours, and some bus routes will run extra service to the cooling centers. The city is also reminding pet owners never to leave animals in parked cars, even for a few minutes, as temperatures inside a car can become deadly very quickly. Relief is expected early next week, when a cold front is forecast to bring rain and cooler air.
clips.L5-P5: Okay, we've seen three apartments, and our lease ends in six weeks. We need to choose one tonight. For me, it's the one on Albert Street. It's the closest to the university, so we could walk to class, and it's only 1,400 a month for three bedrooms. It's cheap, but did you see the third bedroom? It's tiny. There's barely room for a bed. And the only window looks at a brick wall. We could take turns with the small room, maybe rotate each term. That doesn't really solve it. Whoever's in there for exams will be miserable. What about the one on Maple Crescent? All three rooms are the same size, and there's a laundry machine inside the unit. No more carrying bags to the laundromat. It's nice, but it's 1,800, and it's a 40-minute bus ride to campus. 40 minutes isn't great, but we could study on the bus. Not when it's packed at 8 in the morning. Then let's look at the third one on Queen Street. It's 1,600, 20 minutes by bike, and the rooms are almost equal. But the landlord wants first and last month's rent, plus a damage deposit. That's almost $5,000 up front. I can't do that until my student loan comes in, in September. Humm. What if we asked the landlord if we could pay the deposit into parts, half now, and half in September? It's worth asking. Queen Street has everything else we want. Agreed. If the landlord says yes, Queen Street. If not, we go with Albert Street and work out the room problem. I'll email her tonight. Thank you.
clips.L5-P6: For years, high school students in Canada have been told the same thing, to succeed, go to university. Parents push for it, guidance offices are organized around it, and students who choose a trade, like plumbing, electrical work or welding, are sometimes treated as if they've settled for less. I think that message has done real damage, and I'm glad it's finally changing. Consider the job market. Canada faces a serious shortage of skilled tradespeople. Many experienced workers are retiring, and there aren't enough young people to replace them. As a result, a licensed electrician or plumber can often earn as much as, or more than, many university graduates, and they usually start earning much earlier. There's also the question of debt. A four-year degree can leave a student owing tens of thousands of dollars. In most trades, apprentices are paid while they learn. They spend most of their time working on real job sites and only a few weeks a year in a classroom, so many finish their training with little or no debt. I want to be fair. Trades are physically demanding, and not every job is steady, some construction work slows down in winter. And university remains the right path for people who want to become doctors, engineers or teachers. My point is not that trades are better than university. It's that they deserve equal respect. Schools should introduce students to the trades early, through workshops and job shadowing, so that young people can choose based on their interests, not on old ideas about which jobs are good enough.
